After 14 years of Aleksandar Vučić's political dominance, his bloc has lost the snap parliamentary elections. The opposition Student List, which emerged from mass anti-government protests, has claimed victory.

Radio Television of Vojvodina (RTV) opened its news broadcast with footage of celebrations following the Student List's election victory — scenes it had failed to show the previous evening.

“For years, we failed to fulfill our duty. We kept silent, turned a blind eye, reported events one-sidedly, and failed to ask the necessary questions. For that, we owe our viewers an apology,” news anchor Goran Eror said.

Following the controversy, RTV's acting editor-in-chief Nenad Čačić resigned.

A similar incident occurred in Hungary, where state television also apologized to viewers after Viktor Orbán's election defeat.

WHAT LULA’S RE-ELECTION TELLS US: The Class War Need Not End in Fascism

On Sunday, Brazilians did something that the commentariat had told us was a lost cause. On the eve of his eighty-first birthday, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a former metalworker, turned the Trumpist, evangelical, neofascist, Zionist tide in Latin America to get re-elected President of Brazil.

Yesterday, Lula overturned this deficit and won with a margin of nearly four and a half million votes.

I want to use Lula’s victory to tell a broader story. A story about a war, the class war that the few are waging against the many across the Western world. And a story about how that war need not end, as so many now fear, in a neofascist revival.

THE HIDDEN CLASS WAR

“There’s class warfare, all right,” Warren Buffett once said, “but it’s my class, the rich class, that’s making war, and we’re winning.” Mr Buffett was not exaggerating. For almost four decades, Western governments and central banks have pulled every policy lever in the same direction: to make the assets of the few burgeon at the expense of the incomes of the many.

Consider the numbers. Between 1952 and 1988, economic growth explained nearly all the gains of the West’s stock market. From 1989 onwards, growth explains only about a quarter. The largest share, around 40 per cent, came from income diverted from workers to shareholders. Another third came from cheaper money and lower perceived risk. That is not wealth creation. It is wealth extraction: a transfer from those who work to those who own, inflated by cheap money and paraded on the evening news as “a strong economy”.

Then look at the rescues. 2001, 2008, 2020, the British gilt crisis of 2022, Silicon Valley Bank in 2023: each time, the state rushed in to save the asset holders. Together they reveal the rule: to save the economy, you must save the wealth of those who own it – not those who produce stuff, not even productive companies. In the United States, the top tenth own almost 90 per cent of all shares. The Fed and the US federal government insure it for them, doing ‘whatever it takes’ to prop them up whenever their prices tank. The rest of us in the West pay the premium, in the form of the austerity that always follows the bailout.

And the owners need never sell. Why do billionaires pay so little tax? Because they do not earn incomes - they accumulate capital gains, taxed only when sold. So they borrow against their soaring assets at 1 or 2 per cent and live on the loan. Then they die and pay no tax on their capital gains, passing on the loot to their kids at ridiculously low inheritance taxes. Meanwhile, to pay bills and put food on the table, the worker borrows on a credit card at 20 per cent, her debts the mirror image of their fortunes.

Then, a large chunk of these accumulating assets seek even higher rents in places like Brazil where the US government intervenes to ensure that the local governments will also place the defence of these assets’ values above all else.

CAPITAL IS NOT A THING, NOT MERELY AN ASSET

Why does austerity keep returning, even though it is economically self-defeating? Marx tells the story of Thomas Peel, who in 1829 sailed to Western Australia’s Swan River with £50,000 of provisions and three hundred working-class men, women and children. On arrival, his workers walked off into the bush and worked for themselves. Peel had brought money, tools and labour, but he could not bring capitalism along, because his workers had an alternative.

items.tx:
BREAKING: TRUMP BETRAYAL! Zelensky reveals he offered the U.S. THREE OPTIONS to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries — but Trump accepted NONE.

President Volodymyr Zelensky just provided stark evidence of Donald Trump’s betrayal of America’s commitment to defend Ukraine from the Russian invasion of its sovereign territory.

Trump has been pressuring Zelensky to unilaterally stop taking out Russia’s oil refining infrastructure, but the Ukrainian leader said in an interview with the Kyiv Post that the United States has met none of the three conditions he says his country requires before agreeing to a stop to its successful campaign to cripple Russia’s revenue-generating energy businesses. Therefore, the strikes continue.

Here are the conditions that Zelensky said that Trump can choose from to convince Ukraine to impose a ban on blowing up Putin’s petroleum refineries:
Option one: an “energy truce,” where Russia stops hitting Ukraine’s power infrastructure. “That is fair,” Zelensky said, and it’s hard to argue with that. Expecting Ukraine to stop hitting Russia, while its opponent continues to bomb away, makes no sense at all. 

Option two: enable Starlink coverage over Russia so Ukraine can show the U.S. where Russian ballistic missile launchers are and destroy them. Zelensky noted that Trump’s team has said Elon Musk doesn’t want to. Who the f@#k cares what Elon Musk wants? If Musk continues to be an obstacle, the U.S. should nationalize Starlink on security grounds and turn Ukraine’s spigot back on.

Option three: if Starlink is off the table, give Ukraine missiles for its Patriot systems, something that “doesn’t depend on Musk or Putin.” Given the fact that the American military has blown through a significant portion of its arsenal in the misbegotten Iran war, this last option might be the toughest for Trump to fulfill.

“Ukraine had received none of the three proposed forms of support,” he said. “That is why the reaction is what it is. We are fighting for our lives.”
Zelensky also argued the refinery strikes can’t move global prices much, since Russia accounts for only 2% of global diesel exports and the other 98% comes from elsewhere.

Zelensky smartly warned against lifting sanctions on Russia before negotiations, saying they were imposed in response to aggression, “not as a price for the mere opportunity to talk.” He said lifting them early would leave Ukraine without leverage and that rebuilding support for new sanctions after more than 20 packages would be hard, a warning that lands after Trump waived sanctions and tariffs on Russia. “I do not want us to find ourselves without any leverage,” he said.

Meanwhile, the U.S. delegation went to St. Petersburg after talks in Oslo and then gave Kyiv a briefing. Now a broad meeting between Ukraine, the U.S., the EU and NATO is planned in Brussels this week. As long as Trump is in Vladimir Putin’s pocket, however, the prospect for successful negotiations is slim to none.

Of course, the Kyiv Post is only reporting Zelensky’s point of view. The White House has not responded yet to his comments. But one of his points is hard to dodge: Ukraine is being asked to hold back while the other side keeps firing. Only a fool like Donald Trump would expect any invaded country to agree to a deal like that.

items.t: 🚨 Toni Kroos on Harry Kane winning the Ballon d’Or ahead of Kylian Mbappe: “I’ve seen some people saying Mbappe was robbed. I don’t agree. Kylian is an excepti
items.tx:
🚨 Toni Kroos on Harry Kane winning the Ballon d’Or ahead of Kylian Mbappe:

“I’ve seen some people saying Mbappe was robbed. I don’t agree.

Kylian is an exceptional footballer. I know what he can do, and I watched his performance against Barcelona. Scoring twice in a Classico is impressive.

But I think people have become confused about what they’re actually arguing.

Are we discussing who is the more exciting player to watch? Who is faster? Who can dribble past 3 defenders?

Or are we discussing who had the better season?

Because those are different conversations.

I remember something from my time at Madrid.

After one match, we were sitting in the dressing room and one of the younger players was watching highlights on his phone.

He showed me a goal and said, ‘Toni, look at this. Incredible player.’

I watched it and said, ‘Yes, very good.’

Then he showed me another clip.

And another.

Eventually I asked him, ‘Did his team win?’

He said, ‘I don’t know.’

I told him, ‘Then maybe we should find that out before deciding he’s the best player on the pitch.’

He laughed, but I wasn’t really joking.

Football has become very focused on moments.

A player scores a spectacular goal, everybody shares the video, and suddenly we’re discussing whether he’s the best in the world.

But a season isn’t one moment.

It’s what you do in February when your team is struggling. It’s how you perform when the opponent knows exactly what you’re going to do. It’s whether your teammates can rely on you every week.

That’s why I respect Harry Kane so much.

People look at him and see a goalscorer.

But watch what he actually does.

He comes short to receive the ball. He helps his midfielders. He sees passes that some midfielders don’t see. And then, somehow, he’s still in the penalty area when the chance arrives.

I remember playing against Tottenham when Harry was there.

Before the match, we discussed his movement, because you couldn’t simply tell your centre-backs to stay close to him.

If they followed him, he could create space behind them.

If they stayed where they were, he could turn and find somebody running into that space.

I remember saying to one of our defenders, ‘Don’t let him make you decide everything for him.’

He looked at me and said, ‘That’s easier to say when you’re not the one marking him.’

He had a point.

And Harry has been doing that for years.

The difference now is that he’s finally receiving the recognition that should come with that level of consistency.

Mbappe can do things Kane cannot do.

Of course.

But Kane can also do things Mbappe cannot do.

And I don’t understand why admitting that has become so difficult.

I played with Cristiano Ronaldo. I know what a truly exceptional attacker looks like. But even Cristiano understood that football isn’t decided by how impressive you look in a thirty-second video.

You have to produce.

Again and again.

Harry has done that.

And the funny thing is that people are now using Kylian’s two goals against Barcelona to argue about an award that recognises an entire season.

It was a brilliant performance.

But if you need to explain why somebody deserved the Ballon d’Or, you should be able to discuss more than what he did yesterday.

Harry Kane won the award because of what he delivered over the season.

Not because he shouted the loudest.

Not because he had the most supporters arguing for him online.

And certainly not because somebody felt sorry for him after his years at Tottenham.

He earned it.

You can prefer Mbappe as a footballer. That’s your opinion.

But preferring a player doesn’t automatically mean he deserved every award that somebody else won.

I think that’s something football supporters should learn to separate.

Tonight belongs to Harry Kane.

And I don’t think he owes anybody an apology for that.”

items.t: Dear Mr. Musk, @elonmusk My name is Laiza Galvão. I am a Brazilian citizen living in Bahia, and I am writing because of serious doubts about the electronic vot
items.tx:
Dear Mr. Musk, @elonmusk

My name is Laiza Galvão. 
I am a Brazilian citizen living in Bahia,
and I am writing because of serious 
doubts about the electronic voting system used in our elections.

The machines, called urnas eletrônicas, record the votes and send the data to central computers. Many people here, including myself, have looked at the official graphs and numbers and cannot make them match ordinary statistical expectations or the patterns from earlier elections. The curves change in ways that look unnatural, and ordinary citizens have almost no access to the machines themselves, the software that runs them, or a clear view of how the data travels from the polling place to the final count.

Your companies design rockets, build electric cars that actually work, and solve technical problems most governments cannot handle. I am not asking for a political statement or any kind of campaign. I am asking whether a small group of the mathematicians and engineers who already work with you could spend a limited amount of time examining this as a technical question: how the urnas store and transmit the votes, whether the published results can be reproduced from the claimed inputs, and whether the graphs that were released are consistent with an unmodified counting process. A short, rigorous mathematical review that others can check would either confirm that the system works as claimed or show exactly where it does not.

You have often said that verifiable engineering and transparency matter more than institutional assurances. That principle applies here. If the same people who calculate orbital mechanics and battery chemistry can also look at a voting system and its data flows, the result would be useful no matter which side anyone prefers.

I am willing to share the public data sets, the official documents that exist, and any other information that might help. Thank you for reading this.

Sincerely, 
Laiza Galvão 
Bahia, Brazil 
October 26, 2026

items.tx:
One of the funniest moments in A Knight’s Tale (2001) reportedly happened completely by accident during filming in Prague.

The production used local Czech extras to portray the medieval crowd, but many of them didn’t understand English. So when Paul Bettany, playing Geoffrey Chaucer, delivered his increasingly dramatic introduction of “Sir Ulrich,” the audience had no idea what he was saying—or when they were supposed to cheer.

As Bettany continued his elaborate speech, a few extras can even be seen preparing to celebrate before realizing he wasn’t finished. When he finally stopped talking, the entire crowd remained awkwardly silent.

That’s when Mark Addy, playing Roland, stepped in with an improvised, enthusiastic “YEAH!” His unexpected shout gave the confused extras the signal they needed, and the crowd suddenly erupted into applause.

The moment worked so perfectly that filmmakers reportedly decided to leave it in the final cut rather than reshoot the scene.

What looks like a brilliantly scripted comedic exchange was actually a spontaneous reaction to a language barrier, proving that sometimes the most memorable movie moments happen entirely by accident.

The transaction is expected to close before year-end, with GPU deliveries and lease payments beginning in the first half of 2027. Importantly, the $40B figure excludes interest and additional financing costs, with the final borrowing rate still to be determined, highlighting the enormous capital requirements behind SpaceX's AI infrastructure expansion.

Despite the growth, Anthropic reported an $80.7B net loss, largely driven by a $72.4B noncash fair-value charge tied to convertible notes, while its operating loss narrowed to $693M. -International Events-

Iran: Over the weekend, Iran conducted more ballistic missile tests, continuing the trend of earlier last week. Several launches of ballistic missiles were noted at several missile cities, as IRGC forces conducted tests of newer missile components that they have been able to develop and produce during the war. In Tehran, diplomatic endeavors continue as representatives from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey met to further de-escalation measures regarding the war, and to continue the dialog between all parties.

Analyst Comment: This meeting is a big deal as this is the most public effort by Saudi Arabia to seek terms for peace. Mohammad bin Salman (MBS) sending his brother (the Defense Minister) to Tehran on peaceable terms is a diplomatic move that has not gone unnoticed by the United States and Israel. How this works out is anyone's guess, but many speculate that these are the initial first steps toward Saudi Arabia cutting a deal with the Iranians to pressure the Houthis to stop their attacks.

Red Sea/HOA: Houthi attacks have intensified over the past few days, with substantial missile and drone attacks being reported along the Saudi East-West Pipeline. Abnormal flaring was observed at two pumping stations on Saturday, along with several large fires at petroleum storage depots as well.

Russia: The Embassy in Tehran denied reports of evacuations over the weekend, stating that evacuations have not taken place and that they are operating as usual within Iran. Military flights continued over the weekend, however the exact nature of the cargo flights into Tehran is not known.

Last night, former Israeli Defense Minister Avigdor Lieberman formally filed a request within the Knesset to open an investigation into PM Netanyahu on charges of treason, for his effort to restart the war with Iran to disrupt elections.

Analyst Comment: At the eleventh hour, internal Israeli politics are rather important as the political situation cannot be extricated from the military situation. Many of Netanyahu's opponents within the Israeli government have countered his statements on Iranian attack plans, with many critics stating that he's fabricating the threat for political gain. At the moment these claims are unconfirmed, however that's what's on the front page of domestic Israeli news organizations on the eve of their election day.
